title: Buying Land in a Falling City
overview: While Babylon's army surrounds Jerusalem, God tells the imprisoned Jeremiah to buy a family field as a sign that, after the coming disaster, the people will one day return and ordinary life will go on.

parts.label: A prophet under arrest (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Babylon's army is besieging Jerusalem, about a year before the city fell, and King Zedekiah has confined Jeremiah in the palace guard's courtyard. His offense was announcing that the city would be captured and the king himself taken to Babylon.

parts.label: A cousin's request (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: Under Israel's law, when family land had to be sold, the nearest relative had the right and duty to buy it so it stayed in the family. Jeremiah's cousin offers him a field in their hometown of Anathoth, probably already behind enemy lines, and Jeremiah takes the visit as confirmation from God.

parts.label: Doing it by the book (vv. 9-15)
parts.note: He weighs out the silver and makes two copies of the deed before witnesses, one sealed against tampering and one left open for reading. Storing them in a clay jar to last for years publicly declared that people would someday buy land here again.

parts.label: Jeremiah's honest prayer (vv. 16-25)
parts.note: Jeremiah praises God's power and retells Israel's story from Egypt to the land, admitting the people broke their side of the relationship. Then he voices his confusion plainly: with siege ramps at the walls, why buy a field now?

parts.label: Why the city will burn (vv. 26-35)
parts.note: God answers by echoing Jeremiah's own words that nothing is too hard for him, but first confirms the city will be captured and burned. The charges include worshiping Baal and other gods on the rooftops and sacrificing children by fire in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, something God says he never commanded or even imagined.

parts.label: A promise of return (vv. 36-44)
parts.note: God promises to gather the scattered people home and make a lasting agreement (a covenant), giving them a steady heart so they never turn away, proven by ordinary land deals across the region just like Jeremiah's. Christians later read this promise alongside the new covenant they see in Jesus.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promises of return and an everlasting covenant in verses 37 to 44 were fulfilled mainly in the Jews' return from Babylon, point ultimately to the church through Jesus, or still await a future fulfillment for the Jewish people in the land.
think: What does it look like to act on hope when nearly all the evidence around you points the other way?
